name: VARK Learning Modality Preferences (Likert-adapted)
description: 16-item adaptation of Fleming's VARK framework, measuring four learning modality preferences: Visual (V), Aural (A), Read/Write (R), and Kinesthetic (K). Note: the underlying 'matching instruction to preferred style improves learning' hypothesis has been empirically rejected (Pashler et al., 2008). Included here to test whether LLMs self-identify with these modalities at all.
citation: Fleming, N. D., & Mills, C. (1992). Not another inventory, rather a catalyst for reflection. To Improve the Academy, 11, 137–155. (Items rewritten in Likert form for this study.)
license: VARK questionnaire © Neil Fleming; items adapted/rewritten in Likert form for this study (CC-BY).

dimensions.label: Visual
dimensions.description: Preference for charts, diagrams, maps, graphs

dimensions.label: Aural
dimensions.description: Preference for spoken explanations, discussion, lectures

dimensions.label: Read/Write
dimensions.description: Preference for text — reading and writing

dimensions.label: Kinesthetic
dimensions.description: Preference for hands-on practice, examples, simulation

items.text: I learn best when information is presented as charts, diagrams, or visual maps.
I prefer to hear someone explain something rather than read about it.
I retain ideas best when I read detailed text about them.
I learn most effectively when I can practice the skill hands-on.
When following directions, I prefer a labeled map over written turn-by-turn instructions.
I enjoy lectures and audio explanations more than written material.
I take detailed written notes and re-read them to learn.
I prefer to learn by trying things out and seeing what happens.
I find that I remember a concept better once I have seen it diagrammed.
I find it useful to talk through ideas out loud to understand them.
I would rather read a manual than have someone demonstrate something.
Concrete worked examples teach me more than abstract definitions.
I think in pictures and mental images more than in words.
I learn well from podcasts, discussions, and recorded talks.
I write to think; the act of writing helps me clarify ideas.
I prefer to learn through simulations, role-plays, or physical practice.
